paras: The Sunflower Landing smallpox shooting was an attack on an unnamed Black man ill with smallpox, who was shot and whose cabin was burned at Sunflower Landing, Mississippi, as reported in March 1882. The only known account was a single line in a Kentucky paper's news column, which did not say who carried out the attack, when it happened, or whether the man survived.

According to the brief, the victim, described as "a negro with the smallpox," was shot and his cabin was burned. The notice gave no name for him and identified no one who fired the shot or set the fire. Apart from his illness, it offered no reason for the attack, and it gave no date beyond its own publication on March 14, 1882.
No report of an arrest, an inquest, or any official response appears in the coverage, and the man's fate after the shooting is not recorded.

The South Kentuckian of Hopkinsville, Kentucky, printed the item on March 14, 1882, in a "General News" column of some twenty one-line notices of killings, accidents and other events from across the country. Written in the passive voice and without a headline or comment, it treated the shooting of the sick man and the burning of his home as one more brief item of the week. In the same column were notices of three men taken from the Santa Fe jail and hanged by a mob and of three Black men shot by two white men at Arkadelphia, Arkansas. No other paper's report of the episode appears in the coverage.
